query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg‐containing lightweight high‐entropy alloys, the supersaturated solid solution preferentially decomposes during service (or post‐processing) so that Mg segregates into discrete Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds. This transformation alters both the local elemental distribution and the composition of the oxide scale that forms at high temperatures, thereby changing the corrosion behavior and oxidation kinetics compared to the as‐cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non‐equilibrium, as‐cast Mg‐containing high‐entropy alloy (with density below 6 g/cm³) exhibiting a supersaturated solid solution mixed with metastable intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: A controlled heat treatment designed to promote equilibrium phase formation and homogenize Mg distribution.
generation.conditions: A controlled comparison between as‐cast (non‐equilibrium) and heat‐treated (near‐equilibrium) samples when exposed to identical corrosive environments (e.g., NaCl aqueous exposure) and high‐temperature oxidation tests (700–900 °C in air).
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution and redistribution of Mg via the growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic phases, which in turn alters the nature (continuity, composition, and protective quality) of the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: In the as‐cast state, the metastable microstructure permits Mg to segregate during exposure. This localized segregation promotes formation of nonuniform oxide films that may be less adherent or protective (or even promote galvanic effects), thereby accelerating corrosive attack and modifying oxidation kinetics. In contrast, a heat treatment that drives the transformation toward equilibrium phases stabilizes the microstructure and leads to a more uniform, adherent oxide scale that better retards corrosion and oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as‐cast alloy, the heat‐treated (equilibrium) alloy will show a more continuous and uniform oxide layer and an improved corrosion performance (i.e., lower corrosion rates and slower oxidation kinetics) during high‐temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast, non‐equilibrium Mg‐containing high‐entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: Effects are anticipated for lightweight high‐entropy alloys with overall densities below 6 g/cm³, where processing-induced metastability and Mg content drive phase decomposition under thermal or corrosive exposure conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of improvements in corrosion and oxidation resistance is uncertain, as the kinetics of Mg segregation and the nature of the resulting oxide phases may vary with slight compositional or processing differences. Additional microstructural characterization is needed to confirm the phase evolution pathways.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy batch. One set will remain in the as-cast, non-equilibrium state while the other will be subjected to a controlled heat treatment designed to promote equilibrium phase formation. Both sets will then be exposed under identical conditions in a corrosive medium (e.g., NaCl solution) and in high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., 700–900 °C in air).
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion rate assessments (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization)
Mass gain measurements and parabolic rate constant determination during oxidation tests
Pre- and post-test microstructural analysis (using SEM, XRD, and EDS) to characterize phase evolution and oxide scale morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion and oxidation resistance (for instance, showing oxide scales that are as porous or nonuniform and corrosion rates no lower than the as-cast samples), then the hypothesized role of Mg segregation and intermetallic transformation in altering surface passivation is falsified.
